item.title: The Man Who Helped the C.I.A. Secretly Operate in Mexico
item.description:
When the Central Intelligence Agency was looking to quietly expand its operations in Mexico last year, it found an especially useful partner.

Mexico had tight restrictions on how freely U.S. forces could operate in the country. The nation’s president, Claudia Sheinbaum, had repeatedly said she didn’t want them taking part in operations on the ground in Mexico, asserting that it was a violation of her country’s sovereignty.

To the C.I.A., Guillermo Zuany Portillo, a prosecutor and former police commander in the border state of Chihuahua, offered a different kind of partnership.

He could pair C.I.A. officers with Mexican police units on counter-cartel operations — and he was in a bind that made him uniquely cooperative, Mexican and U.S. officials said.

Just months earlier, the United States had revoked Mr. Zuany’s visa because of his suspected ties to the very cartels the C.I.A. wanted to root out, according to a letter Mexican officials sent to the F.B.I. that was viewed by The New York Times.

And the C.I.A. wanted help going beyond the logistical support and intelligence sharing that Ms. Sheinbaum repeatedly said was the extent of the two countries’ security cooperation.

For more than six months, Mr. Zuany shepherded C.I.A. officers as they trained Chihuahua State forces, joined those forces on certain missions and provided expertise during ground operations, according to nine officials and law enforcement officers in Mexico and the United States. In return, officials said, Mr. Zuany’s U.S. visa was reinstated.

Then, in April, a truck carrying two C.I.A. officers drove off a cliff, killing all four passengers. The crash blew the C.I.A.’s cover in Chihuahua and set off a national scandal.

Now, Mr. Zuany is on the run.

A Mexican investigation ruled the car crash an accident, but Mexican authorities this month issued a warrant for Mr. Zuany’s arrest on charges related to his involvement with the C.I.A. They then arrested his former boss, Chihuahua’s former attorney general, César Jáuregui, and charged him with treason, accusing him of also welcoming the agency into the state.

The charges revealed Mr. Zuany’s connection to the C.I.A. But the depth of his involvement with the agency and the fact that the C.I.A. began working with him while he was under active investigation by the F.B.I., as well as many of the details of the C.I.A.’s activities in Chihuahua, have not been previously reported.

This article is based on hundreds of pages of unreleased documents reviewed by The New York Times and interviews with two dozen Mexican and U.S. officials who spoke on the condition of anonymity to describe confidential operations and investigations.

The case shines a light on the Trump administration’s decision to expand the C.I.A.’s footprint in Mexico just as Ms. Sheinbaum was making clear, almost daily, that the presence of any U.S. security forces operating in Mexico would represent a grave violation of her nation’s sovereignty.

Privately, Ms. Sheinbaum has deepened security cooperation, including with the C.I.A. — in part to defuse President Trump’s threats of unilateral U.S. military action against the cartels. But her government has suggested that Chihuahua State officials like Mr. Zuany broke the law by allowing C.I.A. officers to operate without the authorization of the federal government.

Mr. Jáuregui, the detained attorney general, has denied knowledge of the C.I.A.’s presence in the state, instead blaming a state police commander who also died in the crash.

In text messages to The Times, Mr. Zuany said, “I have always conducted myself ethically and professionally.” He suggested The Times reporting was only getting “the version from people who are bitter and acting in bad faith.” He declined further comment.

The C.I.A. declined to comment.

Mr. Zuany has a reputation around Chihuahua. He is known to be well-connected and suspected to be corrupt, according to an arrest-warrant request from state prosecutors against Mr. Zuany, protected-witness complaints and more than a dozen state and federal officials in Mexico who know him.

Mr. Zuany “always made clear to us that he had all the power,” a Chihuahua police official said in testimony included in the arrest-warrant request. “He said nobody was ever going to remove him from his post because he knew lots of criminals,” the official added. “And that woe to whoever betrayed him.”

Four witnesses filed criminal complaints against Mr. Zuany saying he was an accomplice in the 2022 killing of two police officers and then worked to stall investigations into the deaths, according to a complaint seen by The Times. At least one of the witnesses later sought protection from the authorities, saying they had been told that Mr. Zuany had ordered their death, according to the witness’s formal protection request.

U.S. authorities later placed that person into witness protection, according to four people familiar with the arrangement.

Around 2025, the C.I.A. began working with Mr. Zuany, despite warnings about his history from at least one U.S. official and one Chihuahua State official, according to two people familiar with the conversations.

The C.I.A. used Mr. Zuany as a trusted contact on the ground but did not pay him like they do many informants, according to a person briefed on the relationship. While the U.S. military and State Department face strict legal restrictions on whom they can work with, the C.I.A. has a much freer hand and can work with people with checkered pasts who offer access to more significant targets.

In the fall of 2025, Mr. Zuany introduced an American C.I.A. officer to Chihuahua State police officers, according to four Mexican officials. Mr. Zuany told the group that he was there to build a new special forces unit, these people said.

For months, the American observed state agents practice tactical drills, analyzed their equipment and joined workouts, the four people said.

He and some other C.I.A. officers then began riding along on operations, usually alongside Mr. Zuany, according to the warrant request and six Mexican officials who witnessed them. In several cases, the operations ended in frustration when cartel targets got away, the officials said, raising suspicions among some Mexican agents that the criminals had been tipped off.

During one operation, Mr. Zuany and several Americans officers helped lead a mission to detain a cartel boss at a local bar, according to two Mexican officials who participated and two who were briefed. When Mexican forces arrived, the man and his crew were gone, visibly upsetting the Americans, these people said.

The Americans generally wore tactical gear and were armed during operations, though in several cases they wore jackets with Chihuahua State insignia, according to the warrant request and six officials who witnessed them. They frequently carried computers or tablets during operations for what appeared to be real-time information, according to the warrant request and the officials.

The C.I.A. officers did not engage in combat, but instead mostly appeared to provide intelligence and direction, often via Mr. Zuany, the warrant request and officials said.

On the way to one operation in March, Mr. Zuany and an American believed to be a C.I.A. officer discussed how to position state agents during the mission, a Chihuahua official told state prosecutors, according to the warrant request.

In another raid on a cartel safe house, an American officer used his rifle to provide cover from outside as Mexican agents entered, according to two Mexican officials who were present. Afterward, another C.I.A. officer went through digital devices that were seized and was present for the interrogation of a detainee, one of those officials said.

In April, the C.I.A. had its biggest operation yet in Chihuahua: Locate and destroy a large meth lab in the remote mountains.

In the days before the mission, C.I.A. officers met with Mr. Zuany and other Chihuahua officials multiple times, according to the warrant request. Surveillance footage showed some of the C.I.A. officers carrying long guns in state offices, the request said.

Days later, four American officers joined a caravan of more than 60 Mexican security forces into the mountains, according to three Mexican officials who were present and the warrant request. During the two-day operation, the C.I.A. officers tried to conceal their identities by wearing balaclava-style masks, according to the officials present.

The C.I.A. officers helped the Mexican agents locate the meth lab, according to the warrant request and one person present. There was nobody in the lab when they arrived but it appeared to have been active recently, with gas tanks and vats of chemicals, the request said. Afterward, fatigued and hungry, the group departed for the overnight drive back to the state capital, according to the warrant request and Mexican investigative documents on the crash.

The nine-vehicle convoy wound along mountainous roads, led by an armored vehicle that kicked up dirt making visibility difficult, according to the investigation. The truck behind that armored vehicle carried two C.I.A. officers and two Mexican officials, the documents said.

After midnight, that truck drove off a cliff, plunged about 300 feet and exploded, killing the two C.I.A. officers and two Mexican officials, according to the crash investigation. Agents descended into the ravine to collect the bodies, the investigation said.

Mr. Zuany was not part of the operation, but Mexican agents called him from the scene, according to the warrant request and two people present. He instructed them to remove the C.I.A. officers’ bodies and ensure they were not wearing Mexican government insignia, the two people present said.

Mr. Zuany later pressured Mexican agents to conceal the C.I.A.’s presence in the operation when questioned by Mexican authorities, according to three people.

Ms. Sheinbaum expressed fury, saying her security cabinet didn’t know about the C.I.A.’s activities in Chihuahua State. She demanded answers from the Trump administration and state officials in Chihuahua, getting into a public war of words with Chihuahua’s right-wing governor, Maru Campos.

At the same time, Mr. Zuany and Mr. Jáuregui resigned.

Ms. Campos has maintained that she had no knowledge of the C.I.A.’s activities in the state. Immediately after the crash, her government suggested the police commander who died in the accident was responsible for bringing the C.I.A. along on police operations.

Mr. Zuany, in a text message, said that Ms. Campos actually did know about the C.I.A.’s presence. Ms. Campos said in a statement that Mr. Zuany is wrong and should be prepared to testify to a judge. “If he has something to say, he should come forward and say it,” she said.

This month, Ms. Campos and Ms. Sheinbaum met in Chihuahua. Both politicians said they raised their voices in a tense meeting. Shortly after, Ms. Campos’s government issued arrest warrants for Mr. Zuany and Mr. Jáuregui, accusing them of welcoming the C.I.A.

In a statement, Ms. Campos’ office said that the accusations against the two former officials represent “a serious failure” and that “she has taken responsibility for correcting the controls that made it possible.”

Mr. Jáuregui had been running to be the Chihuahua City mayor and was one of the state capital’s most prominent faces, plastered on billboards along many highways. Last month, on one of those highways, he was pulled over and arrested.

Mr. Zuany remains a fugitive.

Julian E. Barnes and Alan Feuer contributed reporting.

item.title: U.S. Army Member Arrested in Britain on Suspicion of Spying for Russia
item.description:
Britain’s counterterrorism police said on Tuesday that they had arrested a member of the U.S. Army on suspicion of spying on behalf of Russia after a joint investigation with the F.B.I. and U.S. military intelligence.

The 41-year-old man was arrested near Gloucester, England, about 100 miles west of London, and was in custody pending possible charges, officials said.

Officials did not name the man but said in a statement that he had been detained on suspicion of violating Section 1 and Section 3 of Britain’s National Security Act 2023. Those sections relate to obtaining or disclosing protected information and assisting a foreign intelligence service. The police did not offer any other details, including about what the man was suspected of having done.

But Brig. Gen. Sean Stinchon, the commanding general of the U.S. Army Counterintelligence Command, said in the police’s statement, “The alleged conduct of a senior soldier, entrusted with sensitive information, is a sobering reminder that insider threats are real and persistent.”

In the police statement, the F.B.I.’s director, Kash Patel, is quoted as saying, “This important arrest involves allegations of espionage, which is of the utmost concern to the United States and our allies.”

Mr. Patel added, “While this investigation is continuing, I want to send a clear message — this F.B.I. has no tolerance for anyone who breaks their oath to the United States and whose actions endanger our national security and that of our partners.”

The Metropolitan Police also said in a statement, “The country to which the allegations relate is Russia.”

The Kremlin did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The man arrested was based out of the Imjin Barracks at the headquarters of NATO’s Allied Rapid Reaction Corps in Gloucestershire, according to a U.S. military official who was briefed on the case and spoke on the condition of anonymity in order to discuss sensitive information. The base is NATO’s largest in Britain and hosts troops from 20 allied nations responsible for rapid response to crises in the alliance.

The counterterrorism police in Britain have investigated several high-profile terrorism cases related to the United States in the past months, including two cases of arrests near air bases in England where the American military operates.

In September, five men were arrested and then later released on bail near R.A.F. Fairford in southern England. Two Latvian men were arrested in October on suspicion of a national security offense after breaching the perimeter of R.A.F. Molesworth, about 70 miles north of London, in Cambridgeshire, England.

In the statement on Tuesday, the police said the arrest of the U.S. Army member on suspicion of espionage was “not linked to any other ongoing Counter Terrorism Policing investigations.”

Valerie Hopkins and Michael Schwirtz contributed reporting.

item.title: On Dakar’s Packed Beaches, Africa Welcomes Its First Youth Olympics
item.description:
Teenage athletes from all over the world have descended on Senegal this month to compete in Africa’s first ever Olympic events, the 2026 Youth Olympic Games.

And in Dakar, Senegal’s sports-crazy capital on Africa’s westernmost tip, the locals are ready.

Fitness and athletic prowess have long been all-important here in Dakar. On any given day, ordinary young people put some of the world’s most toned muscles to work, wrestling, skateboarding, surfing and bike riding.

Women toting goggles and foam noodles make their way down alleyways to the sea to take part in mass early-morning water aerobics classes with energetic coaches.

Groups of men do synchronized calisthenics on the city’s public beaches, hopping backward in low frog jumps and coating themselves in fine sand after sets of push-ups.

Weight lifters lift homemade barbells formed by pouring concrete into buckets and sticking a piece of metal into it to dry.

And every evening, crowds gather up and down the city’s main coastal road — the Corniche — to run, lunge, jump and use the many outdoor gyms that have opened in the city in the past decade.

On a recent evening on Koussoum Beach, hulking men tied traditional loincloths around their waists and between their legs. Then they circled each other, pawing at each other’s hands like cats and pulling each other to the ground.

Beach wrestling is making its Olympics debut at the Games, delighting many in Senegal, where traditional wrestling is wildly popular. Traditional Senegalese wrestling has been practiced for centuries here, and in recent years has become extremely popular and lucrative for top-tier competitors.

“We’re going to beat everyone,” said Zale Baol, a sturdy, solemn-faced traditional wrestler on Koussoum Beach. “Gambia, Ivory Coast, Germany, the United States — everyone. We’re a country of wrestlers.”

He said the key to becoming a successful wrestler was very simple: enough training, and the right nutrition. In the morning, wrestlers should eat Dakar’s favorite breakfast street food, black-eyed pea sandwiches, he said. For lunch, thieboudienne — Senegal’s national dish of rice, fish and vegetables. And for dinner, couscous.

On a recent morning in Pikine, a satellite city on Dakar’s eastern edge, young hopefuls for the beach wrestling team sat on the steps of the national wrestling arena, a Chinese-built outdoor venue decorated with bas-reliefs of wrestlers. They were bracing for the day’s endurance training.

“I’ve been wrestling as long as I can remember,” said Abdoulaye Diouf, 17. He reminisced about how his community used to organize competitions for young wrestlers, rewarding the winners with mangoes.

He winced as he recalled his mother’s wrath when he skipped school to compete in a match. But, he said, “I’ve always been stubborn.”

Dakar and the other two cities hosting Olympic events this year have undergone makeovers in recent weeks ahead of the Games. At the newly renovated Iba Mar Diop Stadium, men shoveled gravel until the last minute.

Many Senegalese were delighted by the new works, saying it was good for a struggling economy, and particularly good for the city’s huge cohort of young people.

“Africa has begun to develop,” said Moussa Thiam, an amateur boxer, on a recent evening.

For some of Dakar’s young athletes, though, the Games remained out of reach.

Over in Ngor, a fishing village of winding alleyways and colorful boats in Dakar, children of all ages glided along rails at Deggele skate park. The park was founded by Moussa Mbengue, who pioneered skateboarding in the area in the 1990s, after a French surfer gave him a board.

Ngor’s most promising young skateboarders, the 15-year-old twins Aminata and Mamadou Samb, had hoped to participate in the Games. Unfortunately, they could not leave the country to attend training sessions that might have enabled them to qualify, according to Mr. Mbengue, their trainer, and Awa Fall, the head of Senegal’s skateboarding federation.

Mr. Mbengue and Ms. Fall each had a different explanation for why the twins were unable to go, and each blamed the other.

But “we are not discouraged,” Mamadou said playfully. “No one in Senegal is better at skateboarding than us.”

Ahead of the Games, few young Dakarois knew how to get tickets to the events, or even what sports would be played.

“I’m only interested in soccer,” said Malick Ndiaye, 17, who had finished school for the day and was on his way to his father’s electronics store in the market. He was pleased to learn that futsal, a fast, indoor version of soccer, would be played.

During an opening ceremony, visitors were transfixed by the choreography, and the voice of the singer-songwriter Baaba Maal blaring from speakers. Lively recreations of Senegalese street scenes showed people selling coffee and fruit.

But away from the venues, Dakar kept up its own routines.

Runners jogged up and down the 198 steps to the city’s giant African Renaissance Monument, depicting a bronze family gleaming in the morning sun.

Others stretched on the sidewalk overlooking the turquoise waters of the Atlantic Ocean and one of Dakar’s most famous buildings, the windswept Divinity Mosque.

“Every country should pray to host the Olympics,” said Zale Baol, the traditional wrestler.

Saikou Jammeh contributed reporting.

item.title: This Defense Makes Drones (and GPS) Think They’re in Peru
item.description:
The S.U.V. in front of us suddenly pulled over. The driver had been trying to lead us to antennas near Kyiv, the Ukrainian capital, that scramble the signals of Russian drones and missiles, but his GPS had gone haywire.

“Apologies. Some technical issues,” texted Serhii, a spokesman for Cascade Systems, the Ukrainian defense company that made the system. He asked that only his first name be used, out of concern for his safety.

We should have known: The S.U.V.’s navigation system had decided that the vehicle was in Lima, Peru, 7,628 miles southwest of Kyiv.

This happens all the time to Ukrainians. When Cascade’s antennas are switched on to misdirect Russian bombardments, the GPS in phones and cars is often misdirected, too — to that particular South American city.

This was now happening to a few of the very guys behind the mapping chaos. They had been hoisted on their own antennas, so to speak.

The system, called Lima for obvious reasons, blasts out electromagnetic interference meant to strip the eyes and ears from Moscow’s missiles and drones, making them think they are somewhere else.

Sometimes, the weapons are so confused to be in Peru that they make severe turns and break apart midair. This has happened even to Russia’s powerful hypersonic missiles, Cascade and Ukrainian military officials say.

But the Lima network has also rewritten the map for getting around Kyiv, suggesting that in any place that deals constantly with drones and electronic warfare, the days of accurate GPS could be numbered.

We were determined to see why, even if we couldn’t figure out where we were.

It’s easy to get sent to Lima.

A colleague’s ride-sharing app told her she would be dropped off at her Kyiv home in 12,276 minutes, after driving across South America, the Atlantic Ocean and much of Europe.

A Ukrainian government official’s Garmin GPS watch said he had run 6.22 kilometers in Lima in 15 minutes 38 seconds, a pace that would make him one of the fastest distance runners ever.

A friend went onto the dating app Grindr to see matches in Kyiv, only to be greeted by men in Spanish. “I’m from Lima and you?” one asked.

Phones don’t always take their owners all the way to Peru. The GPS might put someone in a forest in neighboring Belarus instead of their apartment. On the east side of the Dnipro River, which divides Kyiv, people have found themselves in the Democratic Republic of Congo.

GPS confusion in Ukraine started years ago, when the military first started jamming drones. But it became a bigger problem in August, when the Russians began launching more daytime attacks. On one day in September, alarms in Kyiv lasted for 20 hours. So did the GPS wonkiness.

Increasingly, people are buying paper maps, downloading offline maps that rely on landmarks or trying other hacks.

Lima has become a verb. Food-delivery drivers are Lima’d. Cabdrivers are often Lima’d, especially the ones driving Teslas, which rely heavily on accurate GPS data to manage their core functions.

We got Lima’d on a September evening in rural Ukraine after conducting some interviews. As we drove at a sensible 38.5 miles an hour, an air raid alarm sounded. Suddenly, the Toyota Land Cruiser’s dashboard GPS showed us flying above Peru at 167 miles an hour, about to land in the country’s capital.

Got a confidential news tip? The New York Times would like to hear from readers who want to share messages and materials with our journalists.

Traffic in Kyiv is often snarled, in part because drivers who resettled from other besieged parts of Ukraine do not know how to get anywhere without GPS. When an air raid went off during a recent taxi ride, the driver, Serhii Semerenko, 56, frantically asked about our destination and route. He also tried to memorize his phone map.

“In a moment, all of this is going to disappear,” Mr. Semerenko said. He added: “We’re in Lima every day. And now you and me are about to be in Lima, too.”

This can mess with the most mundane modern conveniences. Ordering an Uber is easy, but finding it is next to impossible. You miss messages sent by your editor in Kyiv’s morning, because it’s the middle of the night in Lima and your phone has gone into sleep mode. (Seriously.)

Ukrainians love a good meme, and Lima is very memeable. People post screenshots of maps showing their locations — often featuring their Garmin running route, which is typically an inexplicable red circle near downtown Lima.

“After the war, I will buy tickets to Peru and I will definitely run around the Great Ukrainian Circle in Lima,” one man wrote.

To get to the bottom of this, we met in mid-October with the commander of the military’s Night Watch unit, who goes by the call sign Alchemist.

Cascade Systems started working on its antennas almost four years ago. Night Watch, a territorial defense unit in the Kyiv region, partnered with Cascade, suggesting tweaks and upgrades.

Early attempts scrambled some Russian cruise missiles and drones. The Russians then figured out ways to get around the jamming, largely by adding more antennas to their drones and missiles, said Alchemist, who for security reasons asked to be identified by only his call sign.

And so it has gone, this war of technology in which each side tries to out-jam the other.

By 2024, Lima was incorporated into Ukraine’s broader electronic warfare network. The latest version, Lima Quant, debuted in Kyiv in August 2025, when Night Watch set up the powerful antennas around the capital to create a networked polygon-shaped dome of electromagnetic noise, Alchemist said.

Cascade Systems and Night Watch eventually decided to trick GPS systems into thinking they were specifically in Lima, instead of confusing signals in a more general way. The goal was to distinguish the system from other electronic warfare efforts in Ukraine, which they said were claiming undue credit.

“We simply changed the signal and activated an Easter egg that had been hidden in the system from the very beginning,” Alchemist said, almost gleefully.

The team initially tried to create separate fake GPS coordinates, known as spoofing, for every major Ukrainian city. One would be spoofed to the Tower of London, another to Mount Everest. “We had the Avenue of the Baobabs in Madagascar, and other places we’d either visited or dreamed of visiting,” Alchemist said.

But eventually the team settled on Lima for all areas covered by the system in Ukraine. It was as good a city as any, and it was very far from Kyiv. It was also now a calling card.

Cascade Systems said Lima diverted more than 30 cruise missiles and 10,000 drones in the first three months of this year. Of 62 ballistic Kinzhal missiles launched into areas covered by Lima Quant, 33 broke apart in midair, Alchemist said. Others were diverted from their targets.

It is not possible to independently verify those numbers. Reports from the Ukrainian Air Force at the time mentioned that some missiles “did not reach their targets,” code language for electronic warfare. Alchemist showed us photos of Kinzhals split into pieces.

Lima’s biggest achievement, he said, came on May 24, when two Oreshnik supersonic missiles were fired toward the Kyiv region. Russia has claimed that the Oreshnik, its newest and most expensive missile, moves so fast that American-made Patriot interceptors cannot stop it.

A Night Guard member used the Lima Quant system to counter the missiles, after warnings from U.S. intelligence about an impending launch, Alchemist said. The first Oreshnik hit garages in the Kyiv region miles from any military target. The second split apart and landed in Russian-occupied territory, Alchemist said. Russia now appears to have mothballed both the Oreshnik and the Kinzhal.

Alchemist invited us to see Lima in action. And that is how we found ourselves behind a Lima’d S.U.V.

Eventually, we ended up in a field where we were ushered, almost reverently, to six Lima Quant antennas. They looked unremarkable.

“There is nothing more interesting for you to see here,” said a commander of a battalion inside the Night Watch unit, Max, who gave us an extremely short tour (and spoke on the condition that we use only his call sign).

The men in the field said they had never been seriously Lima’d. At any rate, they said, the system’s benefits outweigh the costs, an especially convincing argument as Ukraine faces shortages of Patriot interceptors.

Still, there is no denying the inconveniences. One Night Watch member, who uses the call sign Chameleon, told his colleagues about a friend whose new BMW had suddenly demanded a mechanic’s attention.

“It stopped in the middle of nowhere,” Chameleon said. “It said he drove the whole way from Lima, 10,000 or so kilometers, without changing the oil.”

item.title: A.I. and Market Whiplash
item.description:
Last week’s midterm elections were perhaps the first major elections fought at least in part over issues related to artificial intelligence. This year saw record donations from tech executives to tech-friendly candidates. And in some cases, A.I. was actually on the ballot: In local ballot initiatives across the country, people voted to limit or prevent the development of data centers. Many newly elected Democrats have promised A.I. regulation.

If A.I. has surged to the forefront of U.S. politics, it’s in part because A.I. is at the forefront of the U.S. economy. And stock markets around the world rise and fall with A.I. shares, particularly the multitrillion-dollar behemoths based in Silicon Valley. I spoke to my colleague Joe Rennison, who covers financial markets, about the dramatic swings in tech stocks following the midterms and what they mean — for Americans, and for the rest of us.

So, Joe. We’ve seen some serious volatility in the stock market after the midterms. First markets rallied, then they had their worst day in nearly two years. This week, as Nvidia stock plunged because of the Jensen Huang affair, the rest of the market bounced back.

What’s going on, and how much of all this is down to politics?

Certainly some of it is down to politics. The initial rally after the midterms came in part from investors who had parked their cash on the sidelines, in case of some unexpected event — say, a contested election. They bought back in when it became evident we were going to get a clear outcome.

The plunge the next day, though, came after some weaker than expected financial reports from a couple of A.I. companies, and after investors began processing what Democratic control of Congress and some Democratic wins at the state level might actually mean for the A.I. industry.

But markets have rallied since and now seem to be trying to find some equilibrium. I haven’t yet spoken to any professional investor who thinks we’re at the start of a more severe downturn. It’s more that perhaps the first leg of A.I. development, characterized by astronomical growth (and stock returns), may be slowing.

What are investors worried about?

Many people were already worried about the rapid growth in A.I. slowing down ahead of the midterms, and whether the huge amount of spending by A.I. companies would result in big profits any time soon.

Then the midterms hit, and it wasn’t just that Democrats won control of Congress. They won governorships in states that are important hubs for data centers, sometimes by running anti-data-center campaigns. And suddenly people really began to wonder if the rosy assumptions embedded in such lofty stock prices were still reasonable, or whether prices needed to come down a bit.

On regulation, voters seem to want it. But is the U.S. economy now so dependent on a handful of A.I. companies that even Democrats will have to think carefully about regulating A.I.?

I think that dependency is a real concern. Just 10 companies make up roughly 40 percent of the S&P 500, and so swings in the share prices of just a handful of big tech companies can move the entire market.

But it’s worth pointing out that most people who talk about more A.I. regulation or more scrutiny on A.I. tend to talk in terms of slowing down the industry, not stopping it entirely. Some analysts have actually argued that easing the rapid pace of growth would alleviate some of the strains on the American companies driving that growth, and would boost profits and bolster their positions as industry leaders. In other words, a more gradual pace of growth could be healthier in the long run for these companies and for the whole economy, even if it causes some short-term market pain.

How does the upcoming Anthropic I.P.O. fit into all this? It’s another blockbuster. What does its target valuation tell us?

Well, bankers had floated a $2 trillion valuation at one point; ultimately, Anthropic looks to be aiming for just (!) $1.4 trillion, at least for now. So it seems like some of the air has come out over the past couple of months, and that reflects a broader revaluation of public companies. But it’s still a highly sought-after I.P.O., with plenty of investor demand. That’s important because its size means its public debut is not just important to the A.I. industry but to the entire market.

And what about for the rest of the world? Other markets have also had a bumpy ride the last few weeks, right? How much do we all depend on U.S. tech companies, and U.S. politics?

There’s no shortage of examples of the U.S. economy and financial markets driving developments around the world. But in the case of A.I., it’s not just U.S. markets affecting the rest of the world, but also vice versa.

Japanese markets, because of low interest rates, have become a favorite place for investors to borrow money, which is then reinvested in U.S. stocks. Taiwan has the largest manufacturer of chips designed by U.S. tech behemoth Nvidia. And South Korean stock markets have become home to highly leveraged bets on baskets of A.I. companies.

South Korea’s Kospi index fell over 10 percent following the election result, before quickly bouncing back over 7 percent, underscoring how many places around the world have made big bets on A.I., and have a stake in what Democrats do next.

Nvidia’s board of directors was meeting late Wednesday U.S. time to discuss the future of Jensen Huang, the company’s chief executive. He is under investigation for having had an affair with Alice Huang, a woman who U.S. intelligence determined is a Chinese spy.

item.title: Pope Leo XIV Goes Home, Meeting Ghosts of His Past
item.description:
Just a year and a half into his papacy and less than a month after surgeons removed a lobe of his right lung, Pope Leo XIV, the first pontiff born in the United States, touched down in his homeland on Wednesday.

Yet instead of setting foot on American soil, he arrived in Peru, where he spent two decades as a missionary, priest and bishop and became a citizen in 2015.

“Today I understand how much of this land remains with me and how much of my own story also belongs to you,” Leo said, speaking on Wednesday evening to Peru’s president, civic leaders and diplomats at the Gran Teatro Nacional, a theater and concert hall in the country’s capital, Lima. One of his biggest applause lines was when he referred to Peru as “my homeland.”

Having turned out record crowds at Masses in Argentina, the pope flew from Buenos Aires to Lima on Wednesday afternoon, reaching the final country of his 12-day tour of South America. The pope emerged at the top of the stairs next to a sign on the side of his plane that read “Pontifex Maximus,” and was greeted by Peru’s president, Keiko Fujimori, and a chorus of singing children on a red carpet at the Callao Air Base near Lima.

As his motorcade made its way through city streets under gray skies, about 3 million people lined the roads, according to local authorities, holding up cellphones as they waited for a glimpse of the pontiff.

His choice to visit Peru so soon after becoming pope — while deferring a visit to the country of his birth — underscored the deep emotional ties he feels to the place that formed him as a priest.

“That’s a connection that he doesn’t even have in Chicago at that level,” said Raúl E. Zegarra, assistant professor of Roman Catholic theological studies at Harvard Divinity School, referring to the city where the pope spent his childhood and attended seminary.

A ghost of the pope’s past hovered over his meeting with Ms. Fujimori, who was the first woman to be elected president in Peru in June and is the daughter of Alberto Fujimori, the dictatorial leader who ran the country for a decade and was convicted in 2009 of human rights violations, including murder.

When the pope was a young priest named Robert Prevost in Trujillo, in northern Peru, Mr. Fujimori dissolved Congress and suspended the Constitution. The Rev. John Lydon, a fellow Augustinian priest, served with the pope in Trujillo in the 1990s. He recalled that Father Prevost helped organize pro-democracy protests and recruited people to sign a petition supporting the 50th anniversary of the United Nations Universal Declaration of Human Rights.

As a bishop in the city of Chiclayo, where Leo will return on Friday, the pope told Father Lydon — now director of a leadership institute at Villanova University, the pope’s alma mater — that Mr. Fujimori “‘needs to ask pardon for all that he did.’” Mr. Fujimori died in 2024.

Standing at a podium on Wednesday next to Mr. Fujimori’s daughter, the pope seemed to hint at that history. “Past events deserve to be treated with justice and sensitivity, leaving room for harmony to grow and for differences to be addressed with respect,” he said.

In her welcome remarks, Ms. Fujimori, too, acknowledged the country’s painful history. Pope Leo’s visit “also calls us to reflect on our most urgent and pending task: national reconciliation,” she said. She added: “to move forward, Peru needs to reconcile. No country can live as a prisoner of its own wounds. We must learn to look back with truth and justice, but also with mercy and compassion.”

Unlike in the United States, where the pope voted in the midterm elections by mail, he did not vote in the Peruvian presidential election because “it was not possible,” he said to a reporter on the flight from Rome to Uruguay, the first leg of his trip.

Ms. Fujimori was elected this year as a conservative representing the political movement founded by her late father.

Marcela Rios Tobar, a political scientist and director for Latin America and the Caribbean at the International Institute for Democracy and Electoral Assistance, said Ms. Fujimori was a pragmatist who would “try to take as much advantage of this visit.”

Ms. Fujimori’s approval ratings have already fallen in the nearly five months since she was elected president, as voters have expressed dissatisfaction with the economy and crime. “She needs all the help that she can get to have her image boosted,” said Ms. Rios Tobar.

By the time the pope arrived in Lima, the visit had already become politically sensitive for the president. The opposition attacked her for announcing plans to leave for an economic summit in China on Sunday, missing the pope’s departure from Peru next Monday, and opposition lawmakers threatened to block her from leaving the country.

Ms. Fujimori told reporters in Lima on Tuesday that “it would never occur to me to slight our Pope,” but added that she could not miss a scheduled meeting with the Chinese leader, Xi Jinping, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit.

“My heart remains in Peru, but as president, I have state obligations to fulfill,” she said.

In Leo’s speech in Lima on Wednesday, the pontiff was not as pointed as he had been in Buenos Aires, when he seemed to implicitly criticize the economic austerity measures of President Javier Milei.

But he called on Peru’s government to recognize the dignity of work, the need for accessible health services and exhorted all members of the country’s democracy “to cultivate honesty, integrity, and a willingness to engage with others.”

Throughout his papacy, Leo has generally avoided direct criticism of governments, though he tangled with the Trump administration this year over the government’s conduct of the war in Iran.

Mr. Zegarra said that he was not surprised that the pope would temper his words in Peru. As a bishop, Leo was able to express his unvarnished opinions or protest publicly, but, Mr. Zegarra said, “what the pope tries to model as the head of the Catholic Church is to be a figure that can speak to all with decency, but also firmly.”

“He’s taking some distance from his documented history,” he added, “to try to be a bit more of a bridge builder.”

item.title: Strike on Gaza Hospital Kills at Least 6 and Injures 20, Rescuers Say
item.description:
An Israeli military strike on a hospital in the southern Gaza Strip killed at least six people and injured more than 20, according to a statement early on Thursday from the Civil Defense, Gaza’s rescue service.

The overnight strike hit a Nasser Hospital building in the city of Khan Younis, Mahmoud Basal, a spokesman for the rescue service, which is under the Hamas-run interior ministry, said in the statement. The New York Times is trying to verify who was killed in the attack.

The Israeli security agency and military said in a joint statement on Thursday that they had targeted Muhammad Abu Ismail, whom they identified as a Hamas commander “responsible for holding numerous hostages captive,” during the Gaza war.

The Israeli authorities said that Hamas had established a command center at the hospital complex to stage operations against Israeli forces and was storing weapons there. They added that steps had been taken to mitigate harm to civilians.

Hamas said the Israeli claim that the hospital was used for military activity was a “blatant attempt to justify a heinous crime targeting a civilian medical facility.”

In a statement, Gaza’s health ministry condemned the attack, calling it a “flagrant violation of international laws and conventions.” It did not respond to the Israeli claims.

The attack comes more than a year into a cease-fire between Israel and Hamas that has not brought an end to Israeli military strikes in Gaza and that has done little to alleviate the dire and deadly living conditions for the enclave’s two million residents.

Shortly after midnight, at least two missiles hit the roof of a four-story building in the hospital complex, penetrating the third floor and exploding on the second floor in the surgery department, Naseem Hassan, a paramedic and ambulance driver who works at Nasser Hospital, said by telephone.

Israel has continued to carry out frequent strikes in Gaza despite a U.S.-brokered cease-fire that Israel and Hamas agreed to in October 2025. More than 1,600 people have been killed by Israeli fire during the cease-fire, according to Gaza’s health ministry, which does not distinguish between civilians and combatants in its death tolls.

Nasser Hospital has been struck by the Israeli military multiple times since the Hamas-led attack on Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, prompted a devastating Israeli military response in Gaza. More than 74,000 people have been killed in the war, according to the health ministry.

In August last year, 20 people — including medical staff, rescue workers, patients and journalists — were killed in a strike on the hospital that drew a rare admission of error from Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel, who called it a “tragic mishap.”

item.title: A Key Paris Agreement Goal Is Dead. What Now?
item.description:
It was the climate movement’s unifying slogan for the past decade: “Keep 1.5 Alive.”

The tagline referred to the central ambition of the 2015 Paris climate agreement, in which almost every country pledged to try to limit global warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius.

Now, just 11 years after the target was set, 1.5 is effectively dead.

Scientists now say that without drastic efforts to reduce greenhouse gases, it is very likely that the planet will warm at least 2.6 degrees Celsius, or 4.7 degrees Fahrenheit, by the end of the century.

At COP31, the United Nations climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, diplomats who spent so long championing the 1.5 degree target lamented the abrupt setback.

“The world has no chance of holding to 1.5 degrees,” said Chris Bowen, Australia’s minister for climate change and energy, who is leading the negotiations.

Scientists for years have warned that allowing global average temperatures to rise 1.5 degrees Celsius, or 2.7 degrees Fahrenheit, above preindustrial levels would result in a profoundly more dangerous world. Extreme heat will become more common and more intense. Storms will become more powerful and destructive. Sea levels will rise. And poor countries will bear the brunt of the damage.

That scenario is already playing out around the world. In recent months, wildfires have raged from Canada to Indonesia. The collapse of a glacier in Nepal killed thousands and wiped away towns. Floods and mudslides devastated Brazil. And a European heat wave killed an estimated 50,000 people.

In the face of this mounting destruction, one lingering question at the climate talks was what would be the new goal, if any, as the world overshoots the 1.5 benchmark.

“We don’t think that there’s a new target,” said Ilana Seid, Palau’s ambassador to the United Nations. “We still have a Paris Agreement target of 1.5, and so we are still continuing to say that’s the target.”

Rachel Cleetus, director of the climate program at the Union of Concerned Scientists, warned against fixating on a new target, saying instead that it was important to confront what breaching the threshold has wrought.

“I don’t think it’s a question of replacing 1.5,” she said. “There is no new number. We are now in the unsafe zone.”

Leaders rejected the idea of resetting the goal to 2 degrees Celsius or even 2.5 Celsius, saying that allowing for endless revisions created a slippery slope that could make progress harder to achieve.

While world leaders acknowledged they had missed the target, they also said it might still be possible to get back to 1.5 degrees of warming.

The United Nations secretary general, António Guterres, called on countries to redouble efforts to reduce greenhouse gas emissions with the aim of limiting additional warming, and ultimately turning down the Earth’s thermostat.

“The truth is that we have the power to determine how high, how long and how devastating that overshoot will be,” he said. “We have the power to make sure the overshoot is a temporary breach, not a permanent sentence.”

In order for warming past 1.5 degrees to be temporary, humans would have to figure out how to lower concentrations of greenhouse gases in the atmosphere.

That won’t be easy. Emissions continue at near-record levels. Finding a path back to 1.5 degrees would require the world to drastically reduce the burning of fossil fuels like coal, oil and gas.

Although clean energy is growing rapidly, the world is expected to continue to use fossil fuels for decades to come.

Because reducing emissions is proving so difficult, some environmentalists and scientists are proposing different types of geoengineering, including large-scale carbon capture and storage or attempts to reflect the sun’s energy away from the planet by injecting particulate matter into the stratosphere.

“Overshoot must be kept as small and short as possible, and be rapidly reversed,” said Hilda Heine, president of the Marshall Islands, an island nation threatened by sea level rise. “We have fallen short of the emissions reductions needed to stay under 1.5. We must rewrite the future.”

Lisa Friedman and Chico Harlan contributed reporting.

Your newsletter host, David Gelles, spoke to the California governor on the sidelines of the climate summit in Turkey.

What can Democrats in Congress do on the climate front while President Trump is still in office? And what about House Resolution 1, the 2025 budget law that cut clean energy incentives?

I hope the Democrats make this part of their 100-day agenda. That it’s not just rolling back the worst cuts under H.R. 1, that we focus on restoring a lot of the good work that was done during the Biden administration under the I.R.A. and restore a lot of those cuts. Restore a lot of the cuts that were done environmentally in the infrastructure bill that was rolled back by the Trump administration. The clean energy subsidies and tax credits, the work on wind in particular that’s been attacked by the Trump administration, that should all be front and center on our agenda.

Do you think Democrats need to find new ways to talk about climate issues?

You can use different language, and that’s why I talk about places, lifestyles, traditions. That’s why we talk about extreme heat. That is why we have the extreme heat index in California. That is why we talk about climate risks and financial risks. Why we talk insurance markets. Why we just spent the day talking about wildfires and the impacts they’re having on our communities. So I think it’s our language, and for me the number one issue is the strategic imperative now to focus on this transition.

Any thoughts about 2028?

We’ll see. I mean, I still haven’t made a decision, so we’ll see how it all processes and plays out. But it’s all got fast-tracked. That was inevitable in some ways, unsurprising. But I think you’re going to start to see two or three debate stages set up in May and June of next year. And it’s already taking shape. It’s going to be fast.

item.title: The End of Russia’s Bravest Newspaper
item.description:
Novaya Gazeta was a newspaper of near-legendary status in Russia. It was the home of the investigative journalist Anna Politkovskaya, whose books in the early 2000s offered a searing account of human rights abuses, wartime propaganda and corruption in Vladimir Putin’s Russia. In 2006, on Putin’s birthday, Politkovskaya was shot and killed in the elevator of her apartment building. Twenty years later, Russia is back at war and Novaya Gazeta has shut down.

On Monday, the paper held its last editorial meeting. One final issue will come out in the next few weeks. I spoke to my colleague Valerie Hopkins, who was there to witness the journalists packing up their offices.

But first, the latest twist in the Nvidia scandal: Jensen Huang has resigned.

Jensen Huang, the co-founder and chief executive of Nvidia, resigned on Thursday, capping the swift, stunning fall of one of the most powerful figures in the A.I. boom. He had extramarital affairs with a woman who U.S. intelligence agencies concluded was spying for China, and with an executive who reported to him.

Nvidia shares dropped as much as 14 percent, extending a decline that has wiped out more than $1 trillion from its market capitalization in the last month. Follow our live coverage here.

Here’s a visual guide to understanding the scandal:

Valerie, Novaya Gazeta, the last big independent Russian media organization, closed its newsroom this week. The paper and its journalists have been under intense pressure from President Vladimir Putin for decades. Why now?

The real miracle is that they lasted this long. We’ve watched the Russian government systematically dismantle any media organization that is critical of the Kremlin and critical of the war in Ukraine. This didn’t happen overnight.

First their website was blocked, so you needed a VPN to read them. Then they lost their media license. Then Putin signed a decree nationalizing their printing presses. Then this spring, authorities raided the newsroom and one of their journalists was detained and put on trial. The paper was added to the list of so-called foreign agents — this kind of Stalin-era term that comes with many limitations on what you’re allowed to do.

There was this idea that eventually they would give up, but they didn’t. What ultimately forced them to close was when their landlord refused to renew their lease after 20 years and their bank stopped processing the reader donations that were their only remaining source of revenue. They went to other banks saying, Will you help us? But everyone said no. And that’s a function of either direct pressure from the authorities, or the understanding that you’re going to have a problem if you keep working with the paper.

And so they made the decision that they couldn’t go on any longer.

Explain why this paper was so important in Russia.

It was known, above all, for the bravery of its journalists. They were never silenced, despite years of intimidation, attacks, pressure, assassinations.

Six of its journalists have been killed. Shortly after the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the paper’s editor, Dmitri Muratov, was attacked on a train. The attack was so bad that he needed four operations to use his eyes again.

The other reason Novaya Gazeta was so important was that at a time when many antiwar Russians and antiwar journalists left Russia, they stayed. They remained on the ground, living in their readers’ reality. That meant a great deal.

You were in that newsroom during its last day on Monday. What was it like?

It certainly felt like the end of an era. You know, these are people who are full of tremendous love and respect for the craft of journalism. But during that final editorial meeting on Monday, there was also this discussion about the fact that despondency is a sin, as one of the paper’s columnists wrote. He’s an Orthodox priest who was stripped of his congregation for his antiwar stance. So the sadness of the moment was mixed with defiance and pride in having lasted this long.

One of the things I found very moving was the description in your article of Anna Politkovskaya’s office, which had become a kind of museum and is now gone.

Yes, it’s heartbreaking. They saved her office almost as it was when she was killed. They kept her tape recorder, some of her letters, her really old-school computer. Her reading glasses were still on her desk. And then on the wall they had some of her best stories and also an investigation that her colleagues did into her assassination. It was a place where young journalists would come to be inspired. But all of that is going in storage.

I want to come back to the fact that they lasted this long. How did they manage to do it?

They were strategic. They decided, OK, we’re here, we need to follow Russian law. That meant they didn’t write about anything happening on the front line in Ukraine because there are laws in place that make it illegal to cite any sources besides the Ministry of Defense. But they also made it very clear that they weren’t writing about the front lines because of censorship. For instance, they would use the word “war” on their front pages, instead of the state-approved “special military operation,” but deliberately blur it out.

Another thing that might have helped protect them somewhat was the moral weight of their co-founder sharing the Nobel Peace Prize in 2021. And the moral authority of their history: The paper was founded with money from the Nobel Peace Prize Mikhail Gorbachev won. Muratov was close to Gorbachev, and he also knows a lot of prominent decision makers, including in Putin’s government. But as this war goes on, as the screws are being tightened, that will only get you so far.

Is there any other independent news outlet left in Russia now?

There are some, mostly on Telegram, but none of them with this kind of authority and weight. You know, as recently as a few months ago, Novaya Gazeta’s journalists were going to occupied territory in Ukraine. They went to Oleshky, the Russian-controlled city where people were starving, and wrote about it. The type of stuff that Novaya Gazeta was doing, nobody else is doing.

And what will their journalists do now?

I don’t think they plan to emigrate. Maybe they will eventually try to start something new. I think they’re all still trying to figure it out.

This week I went to the opening night of “Owain & Henry,” an epic historical drama about a medieval Welsh prince leading a rebellion against English rule in the 15th century. Stay with me.

The production was unlike any other celebration of a national story I’ve seen before.

It wasn’t “Braveheart,” where the 14th-century Scottish war hero William Wallace famously cried “Freedom!” just before being executed — but ultimately inspired his countrymen to win their independence from England.

And it wasn’t “Hamilton,” where America’s founding fathers won their independence from England and wrote the most ambitious constitution in history (while rapping about it).

item.title: Army Officer Accused of Trying to Spy for Russia Is Afghan War Veteran
item.description:
A U.S. Army officer arrested in Britain on suspicion of trying to spy for Russia is a decorated veteran of the Afghanistan war who was caught in a sting operation, according to two American officials familiar with the case.

The suspect, Lt. Col. Brandon Tyner, 41, was arrested this week. British officials are expected to charge him on Sunday or Monday, and after that, the U.S. Army will seek to charge him under the Uniform Code of Military Justice and transfer him to the United States, the two officials said. They spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss the ongoing inquiry.

Beyond the sting, it was not clear what actions prompted Colonel Tyner’s arrest. He was based at the headquarters of NATO’s Allied Rapid Reaction Corps in Gloucestershire, about 100 miles west of London. The base is NATO’s largest in Britain and hosts troops from 20 allied nations responsible for rapid response to crises.

In a statement announcing the arrest, the F.B.I. director, Kash Patel, said the case involved “allegations of espionage.” Though officials said in a statement that “the country to which the allegations relate is Russia,” it is unclear whether Colonel Tyner actually handed over sensitive information to Moscow.

Cellphone numbers for Colonel Tyner and his wife were disconnected. The Wall Street Journal reported earlier that he had been caught in a sting.

The Kremlin has denied any involvement. “This arrest has nothing to do with us and we don’t know what it is connected to,” the Kremlin’s spokesman, Dmitri S. Peskov, said at a news conference on Wednesday.

Colonel Tyner has been enlisted as a senior human resources officer in the Army since January 2008 and was deployed to Afghanistan for a year starting in December 2013. He also served in Iraq in 2019 and 2020 and Qatar before that. He is the recipient of a Bronze Star Medal and the Defense Meritorious Service Medal, among other awards.

His LinkedIn page indicates that he received a bachelor’s degree in criminology from the University of North Carolina at Pembroke.

In Britain, counterterrorism police have investigated several high-profile terrorism cases related to the United States in the past months, including two cases of arrests near air bases in England where the American military operates.

On Tuesday, federal prosecutors in the United States said that the commander of a powerful Iranian-backed militia helped direct a plot while sitting in a Brooklyn prison against R.A.F. Fairford, a military airfield used by American bombers in the war against Iran. In September, five men were arrested and then later released on bail near the base in connection with the plot.

Separately, two Latvian men were arrested in October on suspicion of a national security offense after breaching the perimeter of R.A.F. Molesworth, about 70 miles north of London, in Cambridgeshire, England.

item.title: Mexican Prosecutor Who Helped C.I.A. Secretly Operate in His State Flees to the U.S.
item.description:
A Mexican former prosecutor facing arrest after allowing Central Intelligence Agency officers to operate in his state has fled to the United States and is now under the U.S. government’s protection, according to U.S. and Mexican officials.

The former prosecutor, Guillermo Zuany Portillo, shepherded C.I.A. officers for more than six months beginning last year as they trained forces in his state, Chihuahua, joined those forces on counter-cartel missions and provided expertise during ground operations, a New York Times investigation revealed this week.

Mexico’s president, Claudia Sheinbaum, had repeatedly said she did not want U.S. forces taking part in operations on the ground in Mexico, calling it a breach of sovereignty. Under the Trump administration, meanwhile, the C.I.A. sought to expand its activity in the country, and saw Mr. Zuany as a partner to help it do so quietly.

The C.I.A.’s cover in Chihuahua was blown when a car crash in April resulted in the deaths of two C.I.A. officers, leading to a national scandal and Mr. Zuany’s resignation. While an investigation determined the crash an accident, the Mexican authorities recently issued a warrant for Mr. Zuany’s arrest on charges related to his involvement with the agency.

Ms. Sheinbaum expressed fury at the C.I.A.’s presence during raids in Chihuahua and denied knowledge of the agency’s activities. On Wednesday, she said in a regular morning news conference that investigations into matter must continue.

“It’s worth finding out who this person is and how he worked with one of the U.S. agencies,” she said of Mr. Zuany.

The Mexican authorities also recently arrested Mr. Zuany’s former boss, Chihuahua’s former attorney general, César Jáuregui, on charges of treason, accusing him of welcoming the American intelligence agency into the state.

The U.S. government canceled Mr. Zuany’s U.S. visa late last year, accusing him of ties to Mexican cartels in Chihuahua, according to a letter the Mexican government sent to the F.B.I. and people familiar with Mr. Zuany’s visa status.

They and the officials spoke on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to comment on Mr. Zuany’s case.

Mr. Zuany did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

After he facilitated the C.I.A.’s partnership with Mexican forces in Chihuahua, Mr. Zuany’s visa was reinstated late last year, Mexican and American officials said.

The F.B.I. had been investigating Mr. Zuany, who is accused of having ties to organized crime, according to the letter from the Mexican government. But the status of the case is unclear. The F.B.I. did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Thursday.

Mr. Zuany recently fled to the United States to avoid capture, Mexican and American officials said, after Chihuahua state police officers arrested Mr. Jáuregui, who is now in a Mexican maximum-security prison.

As of Thursday, Mr. Zuany’s whereabouts in the United States were unclear.

The Mexican federal government also issued an order for Mr. Zuany’s arrest, according to the security minister, Omar García Harfuch, who revealed the information at a daily news conference, in response to The Times’s investigation.

In a statement, the office of Maru Campos, the governor of Chihuahua, said that the accusations against Mr. Zuany and Mr. Jáuregui represent “a serious failure” and that “she has taken responsibility for correcting the controls that made it possible.”

For months, a C.I.A. officer observed Chihuahua state agents practice tactical drills, analyzed their equipment and joined workouts, Mexican officials said. C.I.A. officers also joined Mr. Zuany and police units on operations against drug trafficking targets in the state.

In some cases, the C.I.A. officers were armed while on missions in Mexico, according to Mexican officials who were present.

On the way to one mission in March, Mr. Zuany and an American believed to be a C.I.A. officer discussed how to position state agents, a Chihuahua official told state prosecutors, according to an arrest-warrant request for Mr. Zuany. On another occasion, a C.I.A. officer carried a rifle and provided security as state police entered safe houses in search of drug traffickers, according to Mexican officials who were present.

The Americans generally wore tactical gear and were sometimes armed during the operations. In several cases, they wore jackets with Chihuahua state insignia, according to the warrant request and officials who had witnessed them. They also frequently carried computers or tablets during operations for what appeared to be real-time information, according to the warrant request and the officials.

The C.I.A. officers did not engage in combat, but instead mostly appeared to provide intelligence and direction, often via Mr. Zuany, the warrant request and officials said.

Alan Feuer contributed reporting.

item.title: Nvidia C.E.O. Scandal Sets Off a Blitz of A.I. Memes
item.description:
Jensen Huang and his leather-clad likeness had become synonymous with the technological giant he co-founded, Nvidia. They were so entwined that, this year, the company sold $178 sweaters with a pixel-art version of Mr. Huang on the front.

Now, in the wake of Mr. Huang’s resignation on Thursday after back-to-back cheating scandals, including an extramarital affair with a woman the U.S. government believes is a Chinese spy, the internet has taken ahold of his image to unleash a flood of memes.

In many cases, they are being made by A.I. enthusiasts who revered Mr. Huang.

Images of Mr. Huang have appeared in online parodies of music videos, Bollywood movies, American sitcoms and kiss-cams at Coldplay concerts — many generated using artificial intelligence, the technology that became widely available through the chips Nvidia produces.

The revelations about Mr. Huang, 63, one of the most powerful figures in the A.I. boom, are part of a long list of infidelity scandals that became memes.

Last year, the married chief executive of a tech start-up was caught on a kiss-cam at a Coldplay concert embracing the married but separated head of his company’s human resources department.

Mr. Huang’s image was superimposed on that viral moment by Peter Dedene, a Belgian software engineer. He said in a phone interview on Thursday that he was up late this week on his phone, scrolling the headlines about Nvidia.

Without leaving his bed, Mr. Dedene, 43, used an open-source generative A.I. tool to substitute the couple from the Coldplay concert with images of Mr. Huang and Alice Huang, the Chinese businesswoman with whom Mr. Huang has admitted having an affair.

“I didn’t think a lot of it,” Mr. Dedene said of his meme.

When he woke up on Sunday morning, he said, the post had over a million impressions. As of Thursday afternoon, it had nearly seven million.

“I really looked up to this guy,” Mr. Dedene said of Mr. Huang, adding, “It’s sort of hilarious that, in the end, the technology he cocreated is now enabling these kinds of jokes.”

Social media users have used A.I. to place Mr. Huang in iconic music videos about cheating.

In one post, Mr. Huang, donning his signature black leather jacket, takes Usher’s place in his music video for “Confessions, Pt. II.” (The lip-syncing is better in the original version.)

Thomas Unise, an A.I. consultant in Minneapolis who made the video, said it took him five minutes to find four images of Mr. Huang on Google and feed them into an A.I. tool to substitute Mr. Huang’s image for Usher’s in the video.

Mr. Unise, 40, said the proliferation of memes using Mr. Huang’s image illustrated how rapidly the technology had advanced.

“A year and a half ago, Will Smith eating spaghetti looked like a bunch of smears all over the screen,” he said of the actor and musician. “You can watch a video now and be like, ‘Wow, this actually looks pretty dang real.’”

In another video, Mr. Huang plays the character Neo in a scene from the movie “The Matrix.” President Trump, as the character Morpheus, lectures him on the importance of maintaining strategic competition with China and not falling for the woman in the red dress.

Mr. Huang’s avatar turns around to realize that the woman, replaced with an image of Ms. Huang, has become Xi Jinping, the Chinese leader, brandishing a gun.

Elon Musk also makes a cameo in the meme, which as of Thursday had more than six million views on X.

On the theme of high-stakes deceit in Silicon Valley, some users placed Mr. Huang into “You Can See Everything,” the documentary about Elizabeth Holmes, the Theranos founder who went to prison for defrauding investors.

With the help of generative A.I., users recast a montage from the documentary’s trailer in which Ms. Huang — as Ms. Holmes — unblinkingly insists, “Of course I’m not deceiving you.”

Many of the videos have labels identifying them as artificially generated.

But it’s “still surprising,” Mr. Dedene said of his video, how many people asked: “‘Is this real?’”

Ephrat Livni contributed reporting.

item.title: Paul Barril, French ‘Supergendarme’ Turned Mercenary, Has Died
item.description:
Paul Barril’s offer to African dictators was straightforward: Your opponents will be subjected to surveillance and manipulation. Newspapers will be “infiltrated.” Plots against the state will be “neutralized.”

Plenty of heads of state took up the services he offered, including Omar Bongo in Gabon and Denis Sassou-Nguesso in Congo. Other clients went to Paris to do their shopping at his Security Action Store, which offered the latest in bulletproof vests or night-vision goggles, as Mr. Barril recounted in one of his six autobiographies, “The Elysee’s Secret Wars” (1996).

Mr. Barril was often described in the news media as a former French “supergendarme” for his longtime work in elite units. After he left the gendarmerie, or national police, in 1984, he became a security adviser and mercenary provider across the African continent and was implicated by human rights groups in the Rwandan genocide of 1994.

His death, on Oct. 20 at 80 at his home in Antibes, France, was announced by the French interior ministry. He had Parkinson’s disease.

By the time he founded his mercenary-security company, Secrets, a French acronym for Security Equipment Planning and Realization Company, in 1984, Mr. Barril was a well-chronicled public figure.

In the gendarmerie, which in France is under the military, he joined a new military police intervention unit, the GIGN, in 1974. The French news media chronicled Mr. Barril’s reputation as an ultrafit top cop, a military-grade swimmer and diver, a black belt in karate, a parachutist, a hostage liberator and a policeman working inside and outside the law. With the GIGN, he participated in the 1979 operation against Islamist militants who had seized the Grand Mosque in Mecca, taking dozens hostage.

In 1982, he became part of President François Mitterrand’s special antiterrorism police unit. That year, Mr. Barril was implicated in a murky affair in which he was alleged to have having planted weapons and explosives in the apartment of Irish nationalists in Vincennes, near Paris. French judicial authorities dropped the court case in 2002 on legal technicalities.

“We did the operation. We prevented bloodshed. I don’t acknowledge anything, ever,” Mr. Barril said on the French television program “Tout Le Monde En Parle” in 2000. “I would do the same thing all over again.”

It was in Africa that Mr. Barril gained the reputation that was to keep him at the center of French newspaper investigations, judicial probes and human-rights group complaints for decades.

With another former colleague from the gendarmerie, Mr. Barril was “at the service of the principal despotic governments of Africa and the Middle East, under the forgiving eye of the French security services,” according to the 2021 book “The Empire That Won’t Die: A History of Françafrique,” written by a collective of historians, journalists and human rights activists.

The book called Mr. Barril and his former colleague “emblematic figures” of “Françafrique,” a term employed in France and Africa to designate the murky official and unofficial networks — military, financial and political — entangling France with its former colonies. In 1990, Mr. Barril, for instance, recruited 15 mercenaries to teach the police in Gabon how to use tear gas against demonstrators, according to the book.

His connections with the Hutu government of Rwanda, responsible for the 1994 genocide in which close to one million Tutsis were murdered, earned him his greatest scrutiny.

In 2013, the Human Rights League of France, Survie, a human rights organization, and the International Federation for Human Rights accused him of “complicity in genocide” for supplying weapons and training to the Hutus. French magistrates investigated Mr. Barril’s role in Rwanda for years but never charged him.

Mr. Barril didn’t deny being in Rwanda at the time of the genocide. During a search of the Paris offices of his company, the French authorities found a May 1994 contract signed by Mr. Barril and the Rwandan prime minister in which Mr. Barril committed to supplying the Hutu government with “20 men for training purposes,” “two million cartridges” of varying calibers, “shells and mortars” and “grenades.”

The contract, which noted a fee of $3.13 million, was a violation of the United Nations arms embargo on Rwanda, and it was evidence that his men were helping the killers.

In June 1994, the Rwandan government paid him $1.2 million of the sum, according to Human Rights Watch; but before the contract could be fully carried out, Paul Kagame, who led a Tutsi-dominated rebel group and later became president, entered Kigali, the capital, on July 4, 1994, and halted the killing by the Hutus.

“There were three million dead” during the Rwandan civil war, Mr. Barril said on a television program six years later. “It’s the greatest historical lie ever. They’ve put it over that one ethnic group massacred another, when really, it was the opposite.”

Mr. Barril always hinted to investigators that he had been acting under the indirect direction of President Mitterrand’s administration, which had been allied with Rwanda’s Hutu government.

But his former boss in the GIGN, Christian Prouteau, said in an interview that Mr. Barril’s claims were nonsense.

“He had no mission, despite what he pretended subsequently,” Mr. Prouteau said. “As soon as he left the gendarmerie, at no moment whatsoever did he have a mandate from France.”

“He passed from the light to the darkness,” Mr. Prouteau added.

Paul Barril, the son and grandson of gendarmes, was born on April 13, 1946, in Vinay, in the Vercors region in southeastern France. He spent his childhood in the high Alps, the area where his father was posted.

At 18, Mr. Barril joined the army, was assigned to a tank unit in West Berlin, then returned to France for training at the gendarme sub-officers’ school, emerging top of his class. He went back to West Berlin, where one of his missions was to guard Rudolf Hess, the last remaining Nazi war criminal at Spandau Prison.

Mr. Barril took pity on the old man and, in the first of his memoirs, “Missions Très Spéciales” (1984), fantasized about liberating him. In 1975, he graduated from the gendarmes officer-training school in Melun, France, again at the top of his class.

Not long after Mr. Prouteau helped organize the GIGN in the 1970s, Mr. Barril presented himself in his office, and he became the older officer’s second in command. “He was a flamboyant young officer, brilliant and courageous,” Mr. Prouteau recalled. “He made some dangerous arrests, without arms.”

Things turned sour with the scandal over the arrest of the Irish militants. Twenty years later, Mr. Barril was caught up in another state scandal dating from those years: He received a six-month suspended sentence in 2005 and a fine for having been part of an illegal wiretapping ring in which dozens of politicians, actors, journalists, union leaders and others were bugged during the Mitterrand years.

“You’re not necessarily bugging people to hurt them,” Mr. Barril said on the 2000 television program.

In the meantime, according to Mr. Prouteau, Mr. Barril had gained a considerable fortune working for the emir of Qatar, among others, until illness overtook him at the beginning of the 2010s.

Mr. Barril is survived by his wife, Angélique, and his son, Patrick.

“He always had a nasty relationship with money,” Mr. Prouteau recalled. “And he was fascinated by mercenaries.”

After Mr. Prouteau was shot during a 1980 GIGN operation, he added: “Paul was in the hospital every day. Then, he became the other Barril. I can’t accept that.”

Daphné Anglès contributed research.
